summary: A description of MLTNET, a Telnet-like subsystem for TENEX written at BBN. It lets a user control several jobs on different ARPANET hosts from one console, switching between local command mode and remote mode. It was meant to help with debugging programs that use the network and is simpler than the TENEX user Telnet.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine one keyboard that can talk to several computers at once, flipping between them like channels on a TV. This program lets a person do that.

questions: how to use several remote hosts from one terminal
subtitle: Control multiple remote jobs on different network hosts from one local console.

tldr.problem: Debugging networked programs or running coordinated jobs across multiple ARPANET hosts is difficult when you must switch terminals or make multiple connections.
tldr.mechanism: MLTNET is a Telnet-like subsystem for TENEX that multiplexes the user's console among several remote connections, letting you switch between them like television channels.
tldr.outcome: A user can control jobs running on different hosts from one terminal, with transparent switching and output buffering for each connection.

today: RFC 339 describes MLTNET, a tool created in 1972 for BBN-TENEX users to manage multiple network connections. It is marked Unknown status. Later systems would provide similar multiplexing, but Telnet and terminal multiplexers were more common approaches.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MLTNET (Multi-Telnet) is a subsystem running on BBN-TENEX that lets one user control jobs on multiple ARPANET hosts from a single console. It is simpler than the full TENEX Telnet but designed to be easy to use. MLTNET is especially useful for debugging programs that use the network or for applications that need coordinated behavior across several hosts.

The program multiplexes the user's console, sending input to whichever remote host the user is currently talking to, buffering output from all connections, and switching between them with simple commands.
sections.plainLanguage: MLTNET lets you open several conversations with different computers and hop between them. While you talk to one computer, the others save what they want to tell you for when you look back.

sections.title: Two Modes
sections.content:
MLTNET operates in two modes. In local mode, the user types commands to MLTNET itself, prefixed with <. Commands let you give a connection a friendly name, switch to a remote site, list your current connections, or check network status. In remote mode, keyboard input goes directly to the remote host, and the user sees output from that host on the console.

When output arrives from a remote host while you are in local mode or talking to a different host, MLTNET buffers it so you do not lose messages. The system also transmits special control characters (CONTROL-C for attention, CONTROL-T for time query) transparently to the remote host, making the connection feel direct.
sections.plainLanguage: You have a control-panel mode where you pick who to talk to, and a talking mode where everything goes to that one host. When one host has news but you are talking to another, MLTNET remembers what it said.

sections.title: Commands and Escape
sections.content:
In local mode, commands are mnemonic like ASSIGN (name a connection), TALK (switch to a host), NAMES (list your connections), QUIT (exit), NETSTAT (show network status), RENAME, FLUSH, HOSTS, and HELP. ALTMODE (octal 175) invokes command completion. Editing is supported with CONTROL-A to delete the last character and CONTROL-R to retype the current input.

In remote mode, the user types "!" (bang) as an escape character to change connection settings, like !L for local echo, !U for uppercase, or !S for lowercase translation. To send a literal "!" to the remote host, type "!!".
sections.plainLanguage: In command mode, type short words like TALK or NAMES. In talking mode, type ! followed by a letter to change how the connection works, or !! to send a bang character.
